title: Who chose it
lede: Customers who turned the feature on stayed at 80 % against 50 %. Before you credit the feature, look at who chose it: one real reversal in medicine, then the same 100 customers counted twice, as they chose and by coin flip.

commit.title: YOUR NUMBER
commit.prompt: Of the 30-point gap, how many points is the feature? (0 to 30)

captions: Feature on: 24 of 30 stayed. Feature off: 35 of 70.
The deck says the feature clearly drives retention.
Per 100 customers: 80 stay against 50. A gap of 30.
How many of those 30 did the feature earn?
1991 review: 15 of 16 cohorts found less heart disease.
Hormone users: 56 heart events for every 100 in non-users.
2002 trial, 16,608 women by lot: 164 events against 122.
129 per 100 on placebo. Those who chose it were better off.
100 customers. 30 chose the feature; 24 of them stayed.
Of the 70 who did not, 35 stayed: 80 % against 50 %.
Same 100, split by coin flip: 50 get it, 50 do not.
33 of 50 against 28 of 50: the feature earns 10 points.
Who chose it, and would they have stayed anyway?
HRT was not all selection: when women started may matter.

brand.takeaway: Who chose it is not what it did.

Teaching object (this film's claims.json params): 100 constructed customers with fixed outcomes; people laid out by a mulberry32 Fisher-Yates shuffle, seed 7; coin flip seed 90. Not data.
honest: The 100 customers are a teaching set, not data. Seed 90 was picked because its coin flip comes out exactly even; across 10,000 seeds, 90 % of 50/50 splits of these 100 land between -6 and +26 points. A real holdout needs far more than 100 customers.
The 1991 studies were mostly of estrogen alone; the 2002 trial arm was estrogen plus progestin. The 2004 estrogen-alone trial also found no heart benefit (HR 0.91).

HRT was not all selection: in later WHI analyses, women within 10 years of menopause had HR 0.76, not significant (Rossouw 2007). Per-100 readings of RR 0.56 and HR 1.29 treat each ratio as events per 100 in the comparison group.
